sentences.text: Mahajangasuchus was a crocodyliform with blunt, laterally compressed, and serrated teeth.
This medium to large crocodylomorph featured a broad snout, a massive choanal septum, ziphodont teeth, and a short mandibular symphysis.
The dentary bone possessed 14 alveoli on each half, with the fourth and ninth being the largest.
Its osteoderms featured deep irregular pits over their surface, except at the anterior margin where they overlapped the preceding osteoderm.
These osteoderms had strong keels and were subquadrangular to ovate, suggesting the dorsal armor consisted of no more than two rows.
Mahajangasuchus was an extinct neosuchian crocodyliform that possessed conical teeth.
Mahajangasuchus insignis was a relatively large predator, measuring over 3 meters in length and weighing up to 360 kilograms.
The species epithet insignis is Latin for "remarkable" or "extraordinary," chosen to reflect the specimen's preservation and strange morphology.
Subadult Mahajangasuchus insignis were likely prey for the large snake Madtsoia madagascariensis, despite the risk of injury to the predator.
The genus Mahajangasuchus was described by Buckley and Brochu in 1998.
The largest known specimen, a well-preserved disarticulated skeleton, was discovered in 1995 about 1 km southeast of the village of Berivotra.
The species was formally named Mahajangasuchus insignis by Buckley and Brochu in 1999.
Mahajangasuchus likely lived a semi-aquatic lifestyle, which was a deviation from the typical terrestrial habits of its Notosuchian relatives.
Researchers suggest that the skull palate of Mahajangasuchus evolved to resist torsional forces while feeding.
Research concluded that a large skeleton originally thought to be Trematochampsa oblita actually represented a new genus of crocodylomorph.
The genus was initially placed in the family Trematochampsidae by Sereno et al. in 2001, but later reclassified into Peirosauridae by Turner and Calvo in 2005.
In 2009, Sereno and Larson classified Mahajangasuchus into its own family, Mahajangasuchidae, alongside the genus Kaprosuchus.
Sereno and Larson (2009) placed Mahajangasuchus in the newly constructed family Mahajangasuchidae alongside the genus Kaprosuchus.
Mahajangasuchus lived during the Upper Cretaceous period.
Fossils of Mahajangasuchus have been found in the Maevarano Formation in northern Madagascar.
Mahajangasuchus lived during the Maastrichtian stage, between 72.2 and 66 million years ago.
